title: The first call and Prompt Engineering
why: In the previous lecture we saw how the model works. Today we call it from our API for the first time: we see tokens, parameters and the finish reason not on a slide but in our own code's response. In the second half we learn how to tell the model who it is, what it does and in what form to answer — that's prompt engineering, the basis of every AI feature that follows.
outcomes: call Gemini from your own API with `IChatClient` and keep the key safe
set `ChatOptions` and read the tokens (`Usage`) and `FinishReason` from the response
write a system prompt that sets the assistant's role, topics and answer format
tell zero-shot from few-shot and get an exact answer with few-shot

review.q: What is `IChatClient`, and what do we change to switch from Gemini to another provider?
review.a: one interface for every chat model (Microsoft.Extensions.AI) · only the line that creates the client changes; `GetResponseAsync`, the DTOs and the endpoints stay the same

review.q: With `maxOutputTokens: 15` the answer is empty and `finishReason` = `length`. Why?
review.a: Gemini “thinks” before answering · the thinking tokens (`ReasoningTokens`) count toward the same limit and nothing is left for the answer · set the limit with room to spare

review.q: How is a System message different from a User message?
review.a: **we** write the System message in code: role, topics, rules, answer format · the User message is written by the user · Assistant — the model's answer

review.q: What is few-shot and when do we need it?
review.a: a few “question → correct answer” examples in the prompt · when we want the answer in an exact format or exact categories so the code can use it

review.q: The system prompt says: “You never name a price”. Is that a guarantee?
review.a: no · a prompt changes the probability of a behaviour but gives no guarantee · what must hold is checked by C# code (lecture 19)

options: creates a Gemini client and turns it into an `IChatClient`; takes the key from configuration (User Secrets)
downloads the model to our computer
trains the model on our menu
quiz.explain: `Client` is Google's SDK, and `AsIChatClient` wraps it in the common interface. The model stays on Google's server — we call it over HTTP.

quiz.q: Where is the Gemini API key stored?
options: in the Controller, as a const
in the README, so we don't forget it
quiz.explain: Every other place ends up in Git. Bots find a leaked key within minutes.

quiz.q: We ran the same question three times with `Temperature = 0`. What do we expect?
quiz.explain: A low Temperature picks the most likely token, so the answers are similar. At a high one — different every time.

options: the model spent the limit on thinking and nothing was left for the answer
quiz.explain: Thinking tokens count toward `MaxOutputTokens`. A reasoning model needs a limit with room to spare.

quiz.q: Which is part of a good system prompt?
options: the role, which topics it answers, the answer format and what it must not do
quiz.explain: A general “be good” tells the model nothing. A concrete role, boundaries and format do.

quiz.q: A customer asks the assistant to write a letter, but it's a restaurant assistant. The right behaviour?
options: politely declines and brings the conversation back to the restaurant
quiz.explain: The system prompt must set this boundary: “on any other topic you politely decline”.

quiz.q: C# code uses the review classification: `if (label == "Negative")`. Why is few-shot better?
options: the answer comes as exactly one of the categories, and the code can rely on it
quiz.explain: Zero-shot might write “negative” or a whole paragraph — the `if` won't catch that. The examples fix the format.

quiz.q: How are few-shot examples sent in the prompt in C#?
options: as User/Assistant pairs in the `ChatMessage` list
quiz.explain: For the model this is a “previous conversation”: the User asked, the Assistant answered. The real question goes last.
